k1102: Tirana: liquidity and jobs, at the country's worst affordability
k1103: The capital is where the country's economy actually concentrates — highest salaries, deepest jobs market, the only market where resale liquidity isn't a question mark. That comes at a real cost: average net salary in Tirana runs around €740 a month against roughly €1,900/m² average prices, an affordability ratio that's already among the worst in the country. <s1>The district-by-district breakdown</s1> matters more here than in either coastal city, since Tirana's price spread between districts is the widest of the three cities by a wide margin. Traffic is a genuine daily cost too — 319,000 registered cars and a crosstown drive that runs 45 minutes at peak, in a city whose air quality already exceeds pollution limits at two-thirds of monitored points.
k1104: Rent runs accordingly: a one-bedroom in the centre averages around €680 a month against roughly €420 outside it, and gross rental yield sits somewhere in the 5–6% range depending on which provider's numbers you trust — squeezed lower every year prices outrun rent growth. None of that is unusually bad by regional standards; it's simply the cost of buying into the one market in the comparison with real employment behind the demand.
k1105: Durrës: the cheapest way onto the coast, with real infrastructure behind it
k1106: <s0>Durrës</s0> undercuts both other cities on entry price while offering something neither has: a working port handling roughly 80% of the country's external trade, a university with 17,000–20,000 students, and — once it finishes — direct rail access to the capital. Around half of coastal purchases here are foreign buyers, concentrated among Kosovar, Czech, North Macedonian and Polish buyers rather than the Western European mix Vlorë attracts. The honest trade-off is environmental: Golem's sewage problem and the aftermath of the 2019 earthquake mean Durrës carries the weakest baseline quality-of-life score of the three cities, even where the price makes it the easiest entry point on the coast.
k1107: Vlorë: the best rental numbers, if you can live with the gaps
k1108: <s0>Vlorë</s0> posts the highest average Airbnb host income in the country, and it's the only one of the three cities with a genuine winter economy underneath the summer tourist trade — a working port and a student population that keeps demand alive off-season. Its infrastructure is still catching up to that promise: 24-hour water supply is a project still in its first phase, with real shortages during the 2025 season, and the city's own airport — the story that's driven much of the coast's recent price growth — still isn't flying. The Brindisi ferry link is the one connectivity advantage Vlorë has that neither Tirana nor Durrës can offer: a direct channel to Italian demand that shows up clearly in who actually buys there.
k1110: The Tirana–Durrës railway is roughly 80% complete, with electric trains targeted for early 2027 after repeated delays — a 22-minute ride that turns "Tirana or Durrës" from a binary choice into a corridor question. Stations at Laprakë, Kashar and Shkozet sit on that line and aren't fully priced in yet; once it's actually running, the practical distinction between "living in Tirana" and "living in Durrës and commuting" narrows in a way the current price gap doesn't yet reflect. Vlorë has no equivalent project on the horizon — its own comparable infrastructure story is the airport, and that one has already missed enough deadlines that its price premium is arguably ahead of the facts on the ground, not behind them.
k1111: If liquidity and a job market matter most, Tirana's affordability problem is the price of admission, not a reason to avoid it.
